title: V1 outputs drift toward non-AU conventions (spelling, date format and terminology) despite the target locale being named

observation.summary: 5 of the 10 V1 outputs default to a non-AU-locale convention where the en-AU version differs, despite the V1 system instruction naming the target locale explicitly: a US spelling variant (T02, T06, T09, T10), a US-ordered date (T10, in addition to its spelling issue), or an everyday AU term replaced with a US/generic equivalent (T08). Four of these five tasks are corroborated by both the human evaluator assessment and the independently-run LLM-as-a-judge assessment; the fifth (T08's terminology miss) was caught only by the human evaluator.

alternative_explanations: One content category accounts for most errors: no; the 5 affected tasks span 5 different content categories (food delivery, travel accessories, cafe promotion, personal care, online course), so this isn't a single-domain artefact.

The relevant rubric rule is ambiguous or overly strict: no; 'favorite'/'favourite', 'traveler'/'traveller', 'moisturizer'/'moisturiser', 'Enroll'/'Enrol' and 'March 20'/'20 March' are unambiguous, well-documented AU/US conventions, and 'coffee to go'/'takeaway coffee' is a well-established everyday AU term substitution (see data/terminology.csv); none of these five are a judgement call.

The LLM-as-a-judge is creating the apparent pattern: no; four of the five tasks (T02, T06, T09, T10) are corroborated by both the human evaluator assessment (drafted independently before the judge was run) and the LLM-as-a-judge assessment, with identical spans. The fifth (T08's terminology miss) was caught only by the human evaluator; that gap in judge corroboration is disclosed here as a genuine, weaker piece of evidence, not folded into the corroborated majority as if it were equally strong.

The denominator of ten makes the result fragile: yes, genuinely; 5/10 is a real concentration but a small one, and a different set of ten tasks could plausibly show a different rate. This is disclosed as a diagnostic signal, not a statistically significant rate.

An output is acceptable even though a preferred wording differs: partially; most instances are minor-severity, reflecting that they don't affect comprehension, only locale-appropriateness. The date-format instance is the exception: the judge rated it major (though the human evaluator rated it minor, since '20' can't be misread as a month here), since a misread date is a more consequential locale error than a spelling variant in general. The pattern is worth acting on for locale-conditioning quality broadly, not only where severity happens to be uniformly low.

Does the evidence support a generation change rather than an evaluation change: yes; the V1 system instruction names the target locale but supplies no concrete guidance on spelling, date order, or everyday AU terminology, so the model falls back to whichever convention is more common in its training data. That's a context-supply gap spanning all three dimensions this finding covers, not a rubric problem.
hypothesis: The V1 system instruction states the target locale by name only ('appropriate for the specified target locale') without supplying any concrete guidance on what that locale's conventions actually are. For spelling, date order or everyday terminology with no locale-specific fact given elsewhere in the prompt, the model falls back to its default conventions, which are not reliably en-AU.
proposed_recommendation: Deploy and test a generation system configuration that supplies the en-AU locale profile (data/locale-profiles.json) and matched terminology glossary rows (data/terminology.csv) as retrieved context alongside the system instruction, giving the model explicit spelling, date-format and terminology guidance instead of relying on it to infer conventions from the locale name alone.
expected_effect: The 5 tasks affected here (T02, T06, T08, T09, T10) should show the specific flagged spelling, date-format and terminology issues corrected in V2: the locale profile and glossary are generic mechanisms, not tailored to these particular instances. A null result on any one of them would indicate the retrieved guidance wasn't specific or prominent enough for that instance, not that the hypothesis was wrong.

title: V1 outputs add claims, offers or details the customer's own prompt never gave, in a majority of tasks

observation.summary: 6 of the 10 V1 outputs add a claim, offer, or mechanic not present in the customer's own prompt, most of them specific and checkable rather than generic marketing flourish. The LLM-as-a-judge flagged all 6; the human evaluator's original single-pass review caught only 1 (T03) at the time.

alternative_explanations: One content category accounts for most errors: no; the 6 affected tasks span 6 different content categories (clothing, fitness membership, travel accessories, streaming subscription, cafe promotion, personal care), so this isn't a single-domain artefact.

The relevant rubric rule is ambiguous or overly strict: no; rereading each flagged span against its specific user_prompt, all 6 are concrete, checkable additions rather than judgement calls: T01's 'our best-selling outerwear' and 'made to keep you warm' both violate an explicit 'don't add fabric or unverified claims' instruction; T09's added skincare claims go beyond an explicit 'use that exact wording, nothing stronger' instruction; T03's invented free-class offer substitutes a different commitment for the explicit '7-day free trial, say exactly 7 days' the customer asked for; T06's 'off your first purchase' narrows an offer the customer authorised without that restriction; T07 invents a launch timeframe never given; T08 invents an app-interaction mechanic never given. A seventh candidate, T05's 'Soft, breathable, and made to last', was reviewed and reads closer to ordinary category-typical language than a clear violation, so it's excluded from this count.

The LLM-as-a-judge is creating the apparent pattern: no; each of these 6 spans was independently reread against its own source user_prompt, not just taken on the judge's word, and each addition is genuinely absent from what the customer actually supplied.

The denominator of ten makes the result fragile: yes; 6/10 is a real concentration but a small one, and a different set of ten tasks could plausibly show a different rate. This is disclosed as a diagnostic signal, not a statistically significant rate.

Does the evidence support a generation change rather than an evaluation change: yes; in every instance the model added something the customer's own prompt never supplied, in three of six cases directly against an explicit instruction not to. That's a generation-side restraint problem, addressable by a clearer system instruction, not an evaluation-process problem (a related, separate evaluation-process gap is covered in its own finding).
hypothesis: V1's system instruction says to preserve all supplied facts and satisfy the stated constraints, but never explicitly tells the model to avoid adding anything beyond what's supplied. Left without that constraint, the model tends to embellish marketing copy with plausible-sounding but unauthorised claims, offers, or mechanics, a generation tendency distinct from the locale-conventions gap in Finding 1.
proposed_recommendation: Deploy and test a generation system configuration whose system instruction adds an explicit no-fabrication constraint, for example: "Do not state, imply, or add any claim, quality, offer, or mechanic that is not explicitly present in the customer's own request." This is a different change to Finding 1's locale-profile retrieval and would need its own generation pass to test.
expected_effect: If this hypothesis is right, the stricter instruction should reduce or eliminate unsupported additions across these 6 tasks without needing task-specific patches. A null result would indicate the instruction wasn't specific or forceful enough, or that a single instruction can't fully suppress this tendency, not that the hypothesis was wrong.

title: The human evaluator's single-pass review missed most of the accuracy/addition defect found in Finding 2

observation.summary: Of the 6 outputs Finding 2 confirms added unsupported claims, the human evaluator's original single-pass reference assessment caught only 1 (T03); the other 5 (T01, T06, T07, T08, T09) were missed entirely, surfacing only once the LLM-as-a-judge flagged them and each was independently reread against its source prompt.

alternative_explanations: One content category accounts for most misses: no; the 5 missed tasks span 5 different categories (clothing, travel accessories, streaming subscription, cafe promotion, personal care), so this isn't a single-domain blind spot.

The missed claims are too subtle or genuinely ambiguous to expect a single reviewer to catch: partially, but not fully; T01's fabric-claim addition and T09's stronger-than-authorised wording both directly contradict an explicit 'don't add X' instruction in the same prompt the reviewer had in front of them, which is a directly checkable miss, not a judgement call.

The LLM-as-a-judge is simply more thorough by construction, rather than the human evaluator being undertrained: possible, and worth naming as a live alternative; either way, the practical response is the same, since a review process should catch checkable misses regardless of why they were first missed.
The denominator of ten makes the result fragile: yes; 5/10 is a real rate but from a single reviewer's single pass on ten tasks, not a calibrated miss-rate estimate.

Does the evidence support a generation change rather than an evaluation change: no; the underlying defect has its own generation-side recommendation in Finding 2. This finding is specifically about the review process missing it, a separate, evaluation-side gap regardless of how Finding 2's recommendation plays out.
hypothesis: The human evaluator's reference assessment was drafted in a single pass by one reviewer, an already-disclosed general limitation of this project. Missing violations of explicit negative constraints (an instruction saying not to add something) is a specific, repeatable, and trainable failure mode, not a random miss, since the same pattern recurred across 5 independent tasks.
proposed_recommendation: No system change. Retrain the human evaluator to catch explicit "don't add X" instructions, since that's the specific miss here.
expected_effect: If evaluator calibration on negative-constraint violations is addressed, a future pass over these same outputs should show the human evaluator catching what the judge already did.
